title: Theory Overview
text:
Chapters

01 · What is Machine Learning? · 25 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Frame an applied (clinical) problem as a machine-learning problem by specifying its Task (\(T\)), Performance measure (\(P\)), and Experience (\(E\)), following Mitchell’s definition.
Contrast machine learning with traditional programming, stating for each what is provided as input and what is produced as output (in ML the algorithm is the output, learned from \(\text{training data}\), modelling \(Y \simeq f(X)\)).
Classify a described scenario into the correct learning paradigm — unsupervised, supervised, active, or reinforcement — and justify the choice from the kind and availability of supervision/labels.



02 · Classifiers · 20 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Distinguish a classification task from a regression task by the type of output it produces — a discrete class label vs a continuous value — and identify which one a given clinical task requires.
Represent a classifier geometrically as a function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \{1,\ldots,K\}\) that partitions the feature space into decision regions (one region per class).
Apply the 0/1 loss to a classifier’s predictions and interpret its risk as the expected loss \(\text{risk}(f) = \mathbb{E}[\mathfrak{L}(f(X), Y)]\) — the quantity that training seeks to minimise.



03 · Algorithm examples · 35 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Compare three algorithm families — \(k\)-Nearest Neighbor, linear / Support-Vector Machine, and ensemble (Random Forest) — by the shape of the decision regions each one carves in the feature space: data-defined neighbourhoods around training points (\(k\)NN), a maximum-margin hyperplane \(f(x) = \text{sgn}(w^\top x + b)\) optionally through a kernel-induced feature map (SVM), or many axis-aligned cuts combined by majority vote (RF). Each shape is the kind of boundary that family of algorithm is capable of producing.
Explain the kernel trick operationally: a non-linear feature map \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D\) — e.g. \((y_1, y_2) \mapsto (y_1^2,\ y_2^2,\ \sqrt{2}\,y_1 y_2)\) — can turn a non-linearly-separable dataset into a linearly-separable one, without changing the linear classifier itself; only what the classifier sees changes.
Predict how the accuracy of a majority vote of \(m\) independent weak classifiers with per-classifier accuracy \(p\) behaves as \(m\) and \(p\) vary, and state why the construction only improves on a single classifier when \(p > 0.5\).



04 · Model selection & validation · 30 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Diagnose overfitting from the signature low training error + high error on new data: name the phenomenon, and state its cause — the model has captured idiosyncrasies of the training sample, not the underlying signal the task wants to learn — rather than a fault of the algorithm itself.
Apply the train / validation / test split to a model-selection task: assign each subset its role — training fits the model’s parameters, validation chooses between candidate models / hyperparameter settings, test (held out) estimates the final model’s performance on truly unseen data — and state explicitly why the same data cannot be used both to choose a model and to estimate its performance (every decision taken after looking at a number on a dataset contaminates that number as a future estimate).
Use \(K\)-fold cross-validation as the practical procedure for the validation step: state the algorithm — split the (non-test) data into \(K\) equal blocks; for \(k = 1, \ldots, K\) train on the remaining blocks and estimate error on block \(k\); average the \(K\) errors — identify what the CV error rate estimates (the prediction error of the chosen model on unseen data), and recognise that \(K \in [5, 10]\) is the standard range (smaller \(K\) over-trains, larger \(K\) adds variance).



05 · Deep Learning · 25 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Describe an artificial neuron as a generalised non-linear logistic unit: given a vector of inputs \(a = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)\) and weights \(w = (w_1, \ldots, w_n)\), the neuron computes \(\text{out} = g\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \, w_i\right)\), where \(g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is a non-linear and differentiable activation function — i.e. an old logistic regression in which the sigmoid has been replaced by any such \(g\).
Compose the forward pass of a small fully-connected (MLP) network: given an architecture spec — number of inputs, number of hidden layers and neurons per layer, output neuron — write the per-layer equations \(a^{[l]} = g\!\left(W^{[l]} \, a^{[l-1]}\right)\), identify the activation \(g\) at each layer, and count the total number of weights the network has to learn.
Explain how the network learns: the weights \(W\) are the parameters; each combination of \(W\) yields a single loss value \(L(W)\) — the height on an error landscape; gradient descent updates \(W \leftarrow W - \eta \, \nabla_W L(W)\) to walk downhill — and state why the activation \(g\) must be differentiable (so \(\nabla_W L\) exists at every \(W\) and descent is well-defined) and non-linear (so a stack of layers can do more than one big linear map).



06 · Unstructured data (CNN/RNN) · 20 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Match an unstructured-data type to the right deep architecture and justify the choice in one sentence: multi-dimensional spatial single-information (e.g. a chest X-ray, a CT slice) → Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) because the signal of interest is a local spatial pattern that can appear anywhere in the image, and CNNs encode this via a small kernel slid over the input; one-dimension privileged sequential single-information (e.g. an ECG trace, a clinical note, a heart-rate time series) → Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) because the order of the elements carries information, and RNNs encode this via a hidden state propagated from one position to the next.
Describe the convolution operation on a 2D input: a small kernel \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) (e.g. \(3 \times 3\)) is slid over the input image \(X\); at each position \((i, j)\) the output feature map is \(F_{ij} = g\!\left(\sum_{u=1}^{k} \sum_{v=1}^{k} K_{uv} \, X_{i+u-1,\, j+v-1}\right)\). Then explain — as the core reason CNNs exist — that the same kernel is reused at every spatial position (weight sharing) and is therefore much smaller than a fully-connected layer would be on the same input: a \(3 \times 3\) kernel scanning a \(224 \times 224\) image has \(9\) weights to learn instead of the \(\approx 50\,000\) a single fully-connected neuron would need over the same input.
Describe the recurrent operation on a sequence: at each position \(t = 1, \ldots, T_x\) the network updates a hidden activation \(a^{<t>} = g\!\left(W_{aa} \, a^{<t-1>} + W_{ax} \, x^{<t>} + b_a\right)\) and emits an output \(y^{<t>} = g'\!\left(W_{ya} \, a^{<t>} + b_y\right)\). Then explain — as the core reason RNNs exist — that the same matrices \(W_{aa}, W_{ax}, W_{ya}\) are reused at every position \(t\) (weight sharing across time), which (a) makes the parameter count independent of the sequence length \(T_x\), and (b) lets the hidden state \(a^{<t>}\) act as the network’s memory of everything it has read so far.



07 · LLMs & Transformers · 25 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Decode the acronym Chat-G-P-T backwards, naming for each letter the technical contribution that letter encodes: T = Transformer (the 2017 Attention is all you need architecture — encoder/decoder built around the self-attention mechanism, in which every token’s representation is computed as a weighted combination of every other token in the input, in parallel); P = Pre-trained (the model has already learned a general-purpose statistical model of language by reading a massive corpus, before it sees any user task); G = Generative (at inference the model produces the next token by sampling from \(p(\text{token} \mid \text{prompt})\) and then feeds that token back as input — autoregressive generation, one token at a time); Chat (the model is wrapped in a multi-turn dialogue protocol that keeps the conversation as part of the prompt). A student who can match each letter to its contribution understands what kind of object an LLM is before asking what it can do.
Contrast the Transformer’s self-attention with the RNN’s sequential hidden state from ch 06, on a sequence of length \(T_x\): the RNN computes \(a^{<t>} = g(W_{aa} a^{<t-1>} + W_{ax} x^{<t>} + b_a)\) — position \(t\) cannot be computed until position \(t-1\) has been computed (the loop is serial), and the dependency between position \(1\) and position \(T_x\) has to travel through \(T_x - 1\) intermediate states; the Transformer instead computes \(\text{attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\dfrac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\) where every position attends to every other position in one shot, in parallel, so the dependency between position \(1\) and position \(T_x\) is one operation away. State, as the core reason Transformers replaced RNNs, that this turns sequence modelling into a problem of matrix multiplication, which scales on GPUs in a way that the RNN’s sequential loop cannot.
Explain transfer learning as the operational meaning of “Pre-trained”: a single very expensive pre-training run on a massive generic corpus produces a model that already knows the general statistics of language; a much cheaper fine-tuning step adapts this model to a specific task (e.g. discharge-letter summarisation, ICD coding) using a small task-specific dataset. State the cost/benefit clearly: fine-tuning needs orders of magnitude less data and compute than training from scratch — and that is what makes biomedical applications of LLMs realistic at all.



08 · Using ChatGPT in practice · 15 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Construct a structured prompt for a given clinical task using the 7-slot template — role (who the model is impersonating), context (the situation the task lives in), task (the one verb the model must perform), instructions (the procedure to follow), output (the exact shape of the deliverable), style (constraints on tone, format, what not to add), examples (1–3 worked input/output pairs) — and justify in one line, for each slot they used, why that slot is load-bearing for the task at hand (i.e. which failure mode is suppressed by that slot).
State and apply the competence rule: only delegate to an LLM tasks whose answer you can independently judge as correct or wrong. Concretely: given a candidate task, identify (a) a plausible-looking failure mode the model could produce (e.g. a fabricated citation, a wrong dosage rounded to a plausible number, a hallucinated guideline), and (b) the expertise (clinical / methodological / statistical) the user must already have to catch that failure. If the user does not have that expertise, the task is not delegable.
Choose the right access mode (Web chat / Prompt design / API) for a given workflow and estimate its token cost using the rule of thumb \(1\) token \(\approx \dfrac{3}{4}\) word (i.e. \(\sim 750\) words \(\approx 1\,000\) tokens, \(\sim 750\,000\) words \(\approx 10^6\) tokens). State the decision rule: Web for ad-hoc one-shot questions, Prompt design (still in chat) for a small batch of repeated structured tasks done by hand, API for any workflow that must be repeatable, integrated into other software, or applied at volume (\(\gtrsim 100\) items).



09 · Agents · 15 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Distinguish an agent from a plain chat-LLM by naming the three additional ingredients an agent has: (a) tools the model can invoke (web search, calculator, file-system access, mail client, browser, API call, …); (b) a control loop that, after every model response, decides which tool to call next, or whether to stop; (c) decision points at which the agent either acts autonomously, asks the human for input, or shares state with the human. State the operational consequence: in a chat, every output reaches a human before it becomes an action; in an agent, some outputs become actions without a human reading them first.
Map the four interaction modes introduced in the slides — autonomous search (the agent gathers information on its own), ask for interaction (the agent stops and asks the human a question to disambiguate), ask for sharing (the agent asks the human to provide credentials, access, or a resource), do stuff (the agent performs an action with external effect) — to the two axes that define the trust boundary: (i) reversibility — can this action be undone in \(30\) seconds by closing a tab, or does it persist (email sent, file deleted, record written to an EHR)?; and (ii) human-in-the-loop — did a human read the agent’s reasoning before the action happened?. A mode is “safe by default” if it is either reversible or human-in-the-loop; it is “dangerous by default” if it is neither (i.e. do stuff on an irreversible target without a confirm step).
Place the trust boundary in a small clinical-research workflow: given a multi-step task (e.g. “find the latest guidelines, summarise them, draft a one-page protocol, email it to the PI”), decide for each step whether the agent may act autonomously, must ask, must share, or must hand back — and justify the boundary using the reversibility criterion (“I let the agent search, summarise, and draft autonomously because all three are reversible; I require an ask-step before sending the email because email is irreversible”).



10 · Best practices for ML projects · 15 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Plan a first iteration of an ML project as the simplest model on the smallest sensible feature set, and write an explicit stop-criterion before adding complexity. Concretely, given a problem and a dataset, state (a) the baseline model (e.g. logistic regression on \(5\)–\(10\) features), (b) the baseline metric and the target value that would make the simple model “good enough”, and (c) the single failure mode that would justify increasing model complexity — and not before. State the rationale in one sentence: more parameters and richer features are paid for in robustness, interpretability, and risk of overfitting — so each added unit of complexity must be earned by a failure of the simpler model.
Choose metrics for the problem you actually have, not for the problem accuracy assumes you have. Apply two rules: (R1) on an imbalanced problem with positive-class prevalence \(p\) (e.g. \(p = 1\%\), a rare event), reporting accuracy is misleading because the always-predict-majority classifier reaches accuracy \(= 1 - p = 99\%\) while being clinically useless — use precision, recall, F1, or AUPRC instead, and pick the threshold deliberately based on the clinical cost of false positives vs false negatives. (R2) the data-leakage rule: any decision (model choice, hyperparameter, feature set, threshold) that is taken after having seen a performance number on a dataset converts that dataset into a training set — even if the file is labelled “test”. A faithful test set is one that has been looked at exactly once, at the end, and never again.
Match the interpretability technique to the model family, and weigh the interpretability/performance tradeoff in a healthcare deployment context. The mapping: linear / logistic regression → read off the coefficients (each one is the log-odds change per unit of feature, with sign and magnitude); decision tree → read off the decision path (a sequence of human-readable if-then rules); random forest / gradient boosting → use variable importance (which features the ensemble relies on most); neural network / deep model → use SHAP (per-sample additive attribution) or surrogate models. State the operational rule for healthcare: if the deployment requires clinical defensibility (e.g. a clinician must justify a single recommendation to a patient), prefer a model whose interpretability is built-in (linear or single tree) — unless the performance gap to the opaque model is large enough that the patient is better off with the box-with-SHAP than with a simpler model that misclassifies more often. The tradeoff is a clinical decision, not a technical one.

Total contact time: 225 min.

title: Theory Overview
text:
Course description
A conceptual, applied overview of machine learning for biomedical and clinical graduate students. The module builds from first principles — what machine learning is, and how it differs from traditional programming — through the core families of models and the discipline that makes them trustworthy, up to the architectures behind today’s tools. Across ten storyboard-narrated chapters students meet classifiers and the geometry of decision regions; three algorithm families (\(k\)-NN, SVM, random forest); model selection, cross-validation, overfitting and data leakage; deep learning (the artificial neuron, the forward pass, gradient descent); architectures for unstructured data (CNNs and RNNs); Transformers and large language models; the practical and ethical use of ChatGPT; agents and the trust boundary; and best practices for real ML projects. Every concept is anchored to a clinical application, so that students leave able to frame, judge, and communicate an ML approach to a medical problem — not to implement one (that is the role of the two R workshops).

title: Theory Overview
text:
Intended learning outcomes
By the end of the module, students can:

Frame a clinical problem as a machine-learning problem via Task (\(T\)), Performance (\(P\)) and Experience (\(E\)), and contrast ML with traditional programming (in ML the model is the output, learned from data: \(Y \simeq f(X)\)).
Classify a scenario into the correct learning paradigm — supervised, unsupervised, active, reinforcement — justifying the choice from the kind and availability of supervision.
Interpret a classifier as a partition of feature space into decision regions, and choose performance metrics fit for the problem — recognising why accuracy misleads on imbalanced clinical outcomes.
Apply the train / validation / test split and \(K\)-fold cross-validation, diagnose overfitting, and state the data-leakage rule (any number you act on becomes a training number).
Explain, at the level of why each one exists, the modern architectures: the artificial neuron and gradient descent, CNNs and RNNs for unstructured data, and the Transformer / LLM.
Judge agentic and LLM tool use by the competence rule and by reversibility, and plan an ML project starting from the simplest defensible model.

title: Theory Overview

Assessment
Summative assessment is a Moodle quiz. In addition, each chapter runs one live, dual-mode formative/summative exercise in which in-person and remote students converge on a single shared artifact (a table, poster, or shared document), so that mastery is observable live for both cohorts.

Learning path
This is Module 1 of the course. The path is Overview → Basic → Advanced: the Overview ends (ch. 10) by pre-hooking into the Practice — Basic R workshop, which in turn pre-hooks into Advanced.

title: Theory Overview
text:
Reading & materials

James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. — An Introduction to Statistical Learning (ISL).
Mitchell, T. M. (1997). Machine Learning. McGraw-Hill — the \(T/P/E\) definition.

Lecturer-provided slides (the storyboard-narrated reveal.js deck).

Nota docente: l’header riporta i dati amministrativi ufficiali (Offerta Formativa). Il contenuto erogato è più ampio del blurb ufficiale dell’Offerta — che si ferma a bias-variance e metriche — e include deep learning, CNN/RNN, Transformer/LLM, uso pratico di ChatGPT e agenti: i dieci capitoli qui elencati sono la versione corrente e sono la fonte di verità per gli obiettivi.

Overview → Basic → Advanced. The Overview ends (ch. 10) by pre-hooking into the Basic workshop; Basic pre-hooks into Advanced. Prerequisites are stated on each module page.

title: Machine Learning — An Applied Overview
text:
How the course works
The Theory Overview is delivered as reveal.js slides (also downloadable as one self-contained file per cohort). The two R workshops are ~4-hour live-coding sessions: fetch a ZIP, restore the pinned package environment, and type every line together. See Schedule for the full plan and Downloads to get the materials.

title: Practice — Basic (R)
text:
What you will build
Starting from a real heart-failure clinical-records dataset, we import and wrangle the data (dropping a leaky column along the way), explore it with clinically meaningful summaries, fit a logistic-regression spine scored on two metrics (AUC-ROC and AUC-PR), then tune and compare a small “zoo” of models with a workflow_set, validate the winner on held-out data with last_fit, and wrap everything in a reproducible Quarto report.

title: Practice — Basic (R)
text:
Dataset
We use the heart-failure clinical records (Chicco & Jurman 2020; 299 patients, ~32% event rate), seeded once into data-raw/heart_failure.csv. The outcome is in-hospital death (died / survived). We deliberately drop the follow-up-time column, which would leak the outcome — the first data-hygiene lesson of the day.

Steps

Step 00 — Setup · 25 min
Initialise a reproducible RStudio project from scratch with renv and here.

Step 02 — Clinical EDA · 30 min
Explore the cohort with clinically meaningful summaries (gtsummary).


Step 03 — Logistic spine · 45 min
Fit a logistic-regression spine and score it on two metrics — AUC-ROC and AUC-PR.


Step 04 — The zoo, tuned · 70 min
Tune and compare a small model zoo with a workflow_set, then validate the winner with last_fit.


Step 05 — Reproducible report · 35 min
Wrap the whole analysis in a reproducible Quarto report.

title: Practice — Basic (R)
text:
How to get & run it
You need R (≥ 4.5) and RStudio.
usethis::use_course(
  "https://github.com/CorradoLanera/mlt-overview/releases/latest/download/mlt-r-basic.zip"
)
The download is a bundle of per-step projects, not a single project. Open the step you are on — start with steps/00-setup/00-setup.Rproj. At 00-setup you run renv::init() from scratch (that is the first lesson); from 01-import on, opening a step’s .Rproj auto-activates its renv — then renv::restore() for the pinned packages.

title: Practice — Basic (R)
text:
Course description
A ~4-hour, live-coded workshop in which we build and validate a clinical machine-learning model in R — reproducibly, from raw data to a rendered report. Working hands-on in RStudio, we type every line together: we import and wrangle a real heart-failure dataset (dropping a leaky column along the way), explore it with clinically meaningful summaries, fit a logistic-regression spine scored on two metrics (AUC-ROC and AUC-PR), tune and compare a small “zoo” of models with a workflow_set, validate the winner on held-out data with last_fit, and wrap everything in a reproducible Quarto report. The day turns the disciplines met in the Theory Overview into working code.

title: Practice — Basic (R)
text:
Intended learning outcomes
By the end of the workshop, students can:

Initialise a reproducible R project from scratch — renv for pinned packages, here for paths, {rio} for I/O.
Import and wrangle clinical data tidily, and recognise and remove outcome leakage (the dropped follow-up column).
Summarise a clinical cohort with meaningful exploratory tables (gtsummary).
Fit and validate a supervised classifier with tidymodels, choosing metrics — AUC-ROC and AUC-PR — appropriate to a ~32%-event imbalanced outcome.
Tune and compare candidate models with a workflow_set, validate the winner with last_fit, and produce a reproducible Quarto report.

title: Practice — Basic (R)
text:
Assessment
The official exam method for this workshop is not yet fixed in the Offerta Formativa. The working model is in-class formative assessment: short checkpoints roughly every 10–15 minutes (live environment checks, MCQs with diagnostic distractors, and “your turn” coding tasks), plus a culminating hands-on task in which the class tunes and validates the model end-to-end. All checkpoints run dual-mode, with in-person and remote students converging on shared artifacts.

title: Practice — Basic (R)
text:
Prerequisites & learning path
From the Theory Overview (Module 1) you should arrive with: what supervised classification is and how it differs from regression (ch. 2); the train / validation / test split and why holding out data prevents overfitting (ch. 4); and why accuracy misleads on imbalanced outcomes and why the test set stays sealed until the end (ch. 10). No prior experience with R modelling is needed — we type every line together, live. This is Module 2; it pre-hooks into the Advanced workshop.

title: Practice — Basic (R)
text:
Tools & materials
R (≥ 4.5) and RStudio; the tidyverse, tidymodels, gtsummary, and renv packages; lecturer-provided materials and package documentation. Materials are distributed as a per-cohort GitHub Release (a bundle of per-step R projects) — see Downloads.

text:
Dataset
This workshop loads the heart-failure clinical records (Chicco & Jurman 2020; 299 patients, ~32% event rate) from data-raw/heart_failure.csv (bundled) and rebuilds the random forest live from that data: nothing is pre-fitted on disk. It also adds ~12 synthetic, de-identified clinical notes in data-raw/hf_notes.csv for the LLM extraction step. No PHI is present in any bundled file.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
Steps

Step 00: Recap & setup · 30 min
Rebuild Basic’s validated random forest live and warm up the torch backend.


Step 01: Open the black box · 45 min
Open the black box with permutation importance and agnostic SHAP (kernelshap + shapviz).


Step 02 — Deep learning, honestly · 70 min
Train a small MLP live with torch/luz, then write and shape-check CNN, RNN and fused nets.


Step 03 — An LLM as a typed, reproducible ETL · 45 min
Use an LLM as a typed, reproducible ETL to extract structured fields from clinical notes (ellmer).


Step 04 — Reproducibility capstone · 50 min
Seal the full arc in a targets DAG reproducible with a single tar_make().
Total contact time: 240 min.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
How to get & run it
You need R (≥ 4.5) and RStudio.
usethis::use_course(
  "https://github.com/CorradoLanera/mlt-overview/releases/latest/download/mlt-r-advanced.zip"
)
The download is a bundle of per-step projects, not a single project. Open the step you are on — start with steps/00-recap/00-recap.Rproj; opening a step’s .Rproj auto-activates its renv, then renv::restore() for the pinned packages. Each step is a complete cumulative snapshot (the solution to step N is step N+1).
The LLM step (ellmer) needs an OpenAI API key (optional — it falls back to a labeled cached extraction): copy .Renviron.example → .Renviron and set your key. The key is read from env only and is never committed.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
Course description
A ~4-hour, live-coded workshop in which we rebuild a validated clinical ML model live and push it further. We re-run the heart-failure random forest selection from the Basic workshop live, then we: interpret it with permutation variable importance and agnostic SHAP; go deeper with neural networks; use a large language model as a typed, reproducible ETL over clinical notes; and seal the whole pipeline in a reproducible targets DAG. We work hands-on in RStudio, type every line together, and end with a pipeline we can explain, extend, and re-run.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
Intended learning outcomes
By the end of the workshop, students can:

Interpret a fitted model with permutation variable importance and agnostic SHAP (kernelshap + shapviz), anchored by a logistic permshap() sanity-check.
Train a small MLP with torch / luz, and read and shape-check CNN, RNN, and fused architectures (written-not-trained, so class stays on schedule).
Use an LLM (ellmer) as a typed, reproducible ETL to extract structured fields from synthetic clinical notes.
Assemble a reproducible targets pipeline that re-runs the full arc (raw data to interpreted predictions) with a single tar_make().
Weigh the interpretability / performance trade-off in a clinical-deployment context.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
Steps & schedule
The five steps and their contact time are on the Schedule page:

Step 00 · Recap & setup: 30 min
Step 01 · Open the black box: 45 min
Step 02 · Deep learning: 70 min
Step 03 · An LLM as a typed, reproducible ETL: 45 min
Step 04 · Reproducibility capstone: 50 min

Total ≈ 240 min, within the 10 officially allocated hours.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
Dataset
The workshop loads the heart-failure clinical records (Chicco & Jurman 2020; 299 patients, ~32% event rate) from data-raw/heart_failure.csv (bundled) and rebuilds the random forest live from that data: nothing is pre-fitted on disk. It adds ~12 synthetic, de-identified clinical notes in data-raw/hf_notes.csv for the LLM extraction step. No PHI is present in any bundled file.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
Assessment
As for the Basic workshop, the official exam method is not yet fixed in the Offerta Formativa. The working model is in-class formative assessment (dual-mode checkpoints throughout) plus a hands-on reproducibility capstone (the targets DAG) as the culminating task.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
Prerequisites & learning path
You must have completed the Basic workshop (Module 2): the validated random forest it produces is the starting point here (rebuilt live from the bundled data, so you do not need the model on disk). From the Theory Overview the relevant background is model interpretability (ch. 4, revisited ch. 10), the neural network (ch. 5), CNN/RNN architectures (ch. 6), and what an LLM is (ch. 7). This is Module 3, the final module.

title: Practice — Advanced (R)
text:
Tools & materials
R (≥ 4.5) and RStudio; tidymodels, vip, kernelshap, shapviz, torch, luz, brulee, ellmer, targets, and tarchetypes. The LLM step optionally uses an OPENAI_API_KEY (set locally in .Renviron, never committed); without a key it falls back to a labeled cached extraction so the workshop can continue. Lecturer materials and package documentation complete the set. Materials are distributed as a per-cohort GitHub Release; see Downloads.
Nota docente: il blurb ufficiale dell’Offerta (random forest / gradient boosting / unsupervised / feature engineering) è ormai datato rispetto all’arco erogato: interpretabilità con SHAP, deep learning con torch, ETL con LLM (ellmer), pipeline targets. Il contenuto erogato è quello corrente e intenzionale; l’header riporta i dati amministrativi ufficiali.

title: Schedule & Planning
text: Module 1 · Theory Overview

title: Schedule & Planning
text:
Chapters

01 · What is Machine Learning? · 25 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Frame an applied (clinical) problem as a machine-learning problem by specifying its Task (\(T\)), Performance measure (\(P\)), and Experience (\(E\)), following Mitchell’s definition.
Contrast machine learning with traditional programming, stating for each what is provided as input and what is produced as output (in ML the algorithm is the output, learned from \(\text{training data}\), modelling \(Y \simeq f(X)\)).
Classify a described scenario into the correct learning paradigm — unsupervised, supervised, active, or reinforcement — and justify the choice from the kind and availability of supervision/labels.



02 · Classifiers · 20 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Distinguish a classification task from a regression task by the type of output it produces — a discrete class label vs a continuous value — and identify which one a given clinical task requires.
Represent a classifier geometrically as a function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \{1,\ldots,K\}\) that partitions the feature space into decision regions (one region per class).
Apply the 0/1 loss to a classifier’s predictions and interpret its risk as the expected loss \(\text{risk}(f) = \mathbb{E}[\mathfrak{L}(f(X), Y)]\) — the quantity that training seeks to minimise.



03 · Algorithm examples · 35 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Compare three algorithm families — \(k\)-Nearest Neighbor, linear / Support-Vector Machine, and ensemble (Random Forest) — by the shape of the decision regions each one carves in the feature space: data-defined neighbourhoods around training points (\(k\)NN), a maximum-margin hyperplane \(f(x) = \text{sgn}(w^\top x + b)\) optionally through a kernel-induced feature map (SVM), or many axis-aligned cuts combined by majority vote (RF). Each shape is the kind of boundary that family of algorithm is capable of producing.
Explain the kernel trick operationally: a non-linear feature map \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D\) — e.g. \((y_1, y_2) \mapsto (y_1^2,\ y_2^2,\ \sqrt{2}\,y_1 y_2)\) — can turn a non-linearly-separable dataset into a linearly-separable one, without changing the linear classifier itself; only what the classifier sees changes.
Predict how the accuracy of a majority vote of \(m\) independent weak classifiers with per-classifier accuracy \(p\) behaves as \(m\) and \(p\) vary, and state why the construction only improves on a single classifier when \(p > 0.5\).



04 · Model selection & validation · 30 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Diagnose overfitting from the signature low training error + high error on new data: name the phenomenon, and state its cause — the model has captured idiosyncrasies of the training sample, not the underlying signal the task wants to learn — rather than a fault of the algorithm itself.
Apply the train / validation / test split to a model-selection task: assign each subset its role — training fits the model’s parameters, validation chooses between candidate models / hyperparameter settings, test (held out) estimates the final model’s performance on truly unseen data — and state explicitly why the same data cannot be used both to choose a model and to estimate its performance (every decision taken after looking at a number on a dataset contaminates that number as a future estimate).
Use \(K\)-fold cross-validation as the practical procedure for the validation step: state the algorithm — split the (non-test) data into \(K\) equal blocks; for \(k = 1, \ldots, K\) train on the remaining blocks and estimate error on block \(k\); average the \(K\) errors — identify what the CV error rate estimates (the prediction error of the chosen model on unseen data), and recognise that \(K \in [5, 10]\) is the standard range (smaller \(K\) over-trains, larger \(K\) adds variance).



05 · Deep Learning · 25 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Describe an artificial neuron as a generalised non-linear logistic unit: given a vector of inputs \(a = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)\) and weights \(w = (w_1, \ldots, w_n)\), the neuron computes \(\text{out} = g\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \, w_i\right)\), where \(g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is a non-linear and differentiable activation function — i.e. an old logistic regression in which the sigmoid has been replaced by any such \(g\).
Compose the forward pass of a small fully-connected (MLP) network: given an architecture spec — number of inputs, number of hidden layers and neurons per layer, output neuron — write the per-layer equations \(a^{[l]} = g\!\left(W^{[l]} \, a^{[l-1]}\right)\), identify the activation \(g\) at each layer, and count the total number of weights the network has to learn.
Explain how the network learns: the weights \(W\) are the parameters; each combination of \(W\) yields a single loss value \(L(W)\) — the height on an error landscape; gradient descent updates \(W \leftarrow W - \eta \, \nabla_W L(W)\) to walk downhill — and state why the activation \(g\) must be differentiable (so \(\nabla_W L\) exists at every \(W\) and descent is well-defined) and non-linear (so a stack of layers can do more than one big linear map).



06 · Unstructured data (CNN/RNN) · 20 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Match an unstructured-data type to the right deep architecture and justify the choice in one sentence: multi-dimensional spatial single-information (e.g. a chest X-ray, a CT slice) → Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) because the signal of interest is a local spatial pattern that can appear anywhere in the image, and CNNs encode this via a small kernel slid over the input; one-dimension privileged sequential single-information (e.g. an ECG trace, a clinical note, a heart-rate time series) → Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) because the order of the elements carries information, and RNNs encode this via a hidden state propagated from one position to the next.
Describe the convolution operation on a 2D input: a small kernel \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) (e.g. \(3 \times 3\)) is slid over the input image \(X\); at each position \((i, j)\) the output feature map is \(F_{ij} = g\!\left(\sum_{u=1}^{k} \sum_{v=1}^{k} K_{uv} \, X_{i+u-1,\, j+v-1}\right)\). Then explain — as the core reason CNNs exist — that the same kernel is reused at every spatial position (weight sharing) and is therefore much smaller than a fully-connected layer would be on the same input: a \(3 \times 3\) kernel scanning a \(224 \times 224\) image has \(9\) weights to learn instead of the \(\approx 50\,000\) a single fully-connected neuron would need over the same input.
Describe the recurrent operation on a sequence: at each position \(t = 1, \ldots, T_x\) the network updates a hidden activation \(a^{<t>} = g\!\left(W_{aa} \, a^{<t-1>} + W_{ax} \, x^{<t>} + b_a\right)\) and emits an output \(y^{<t>} = g'\!\left(W_{ya} \, a^{<t>} + b_y\right)\). Then explain — as the core reason RNNs exist — that the same matrices \(W_{aa}, W_{ax}, W_{ya}\) are reused at every position \(t\) (weight sharing across time), which (a) makes the parameter count independent of the sequence length \(T_x\), and (b) lets the hidden state \(a^{<t>}\) act as the network’s memory of everything it has read so far.



07 · LLMs & Transformers · 25 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Decode the acronym Chat-G-P-T backwards, naming for each letter the technical contribution that letter encodes: T = Transformer (the 2017 Attention is all you need architecture — encoder/decoder built around the self-attention mechanism, in which every token’s representation is computed as a weighted combination of every other token in the input, in parallel); P = Pre-trained (the model has already learned a general-purpose statistical model of language by reading a massive corpus, before it sees any user task); G = Generative (at inference the model produces the next token by sampling from \(p(\text{token} \mid \text{prompt})\) and then feeds that token back as input — autoregressive generation, one token at a time); Chat (the model is wrapped in a multi-turn dialogue protocol that keeps the conversation as part of the prompt). A student who can match each letter to its contribution understands what kind of object an LLM is before asking what it can do.
Contrast the Transformer’s self-attention with the RNN’s sequential hidden state from ch 06, on a sequence of length \(T_x\): the RNN computes \(a^{<t>} = g(W_{aa} a^{<t-1>} + W_{ax} x^{<t>} + b_a)\) — position \(t\) cannot be computed until position \(t-1\) has been computed (the loop is serial), and the dependency between position \(1\) and position \(T_x\) has to travel through \(T_x - 1\) intermediate states; the Transformer instead computes \(\text{attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\dfrac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\) where every position attends to every other position in one shot, in parallel, so the dependency between position \(1\) and position \(T_x\) is one operation away. State, as the core reason Transformers replaced RNNs, that this turns sequence modelling into a problem of matrix multiplication, which scales on GPUs in a way that the RNN’s sequential loop cannot.
Explain transfer learning as the operational meaning of “Pre-trained”: a single very expensive pre-training run on a massive generic corpus produces a model that already knows the general statistics of language; a much cheaper fine-tuning step adapts this model to a specific task (e.g. discharge-letter summarisation, ICD coding) using a small task-specific dataset. State the cost/benefit clearly: fine-tuning needs orders of magnitude less data and compute than training from scratch — and that is what makes biomedical applications of LLMs realistic at all.



08 · Using ChatGPT in practice · 15 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Construct a structured prompt for a given clinical task using the 7-slot template — role (who the model is impersonating), context (the situation the task lives in), task (the one verb the model must perform), instructions (the procedure to follow), output (the exact shape of the deliverable), style (constraints on tone, format, what not to add), examples (1–3 worked input/output pairs) — and justify in one line, for each slot they used, why that slot is load-bearing for the task at hand (i.e. which failure mode is suppressed by that slot).
State and apply the competence rule: only delegate to an LLM tasks whose answer you can independently judge as correct or wrong. Concretely: given a candidate task, identify (a) a plausible-looking failure mode the model could produce (e.g. a fabricated citation, a wrong dosage rounded to a plausible number, a hallucinated guideline), and (b) the expertise (clinical / methodological / statistical) the user must already have to catch that failure. If the user does not have that expertise, the task is not delegable.
Choose the right access mode (Web chat / Prompt design / API) for a given workflow and estimate its token cost using the rule of thumb \(1\) token \(\approx \dfrac{3}{4}\) word (i.e. \(\sim 750\) words \(\approx 1\,000\) tokens, \(\sim 750\,000\) words \(\approx 10^6\) tokens). State the decision rule: Web for ad-hoc one-shot questions, Prompt design (still in chat) for a small batch of repeated structured tasks done by hand, API for any workflow that must be repeatable, integrated into other software, or applied at volume (\(\gtrsim 100\) items).



09 · Agents · 15 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Distinguish an agent from a plain chat-LLM by naming the three additional ingredients an agent has: (a) tools the model can invoke (web search, calculator, file-system access, mail client, browser, API call, …); (b) a control loop that, after every model response, decides which tool to call next, or whether to stop; (c) decision points at which the agent either acts autonomously, asks the human for input, or shares state with the human. State the operational consequence: in a chat, every output reaches a human before it becomes an action; in an agent, some outputs become actions without a human reading them first.
Map the four interaction modes introduced in the slides — autonomous search (the agent gathers information on its own), ask for interaction (the agent stops and asks the human a question to disambiguate), ask for sharing (the agent asks the human to provide credentials, access, or a resource), do stuff (the agent performs an action with external effect) — to the two axes that define the trust boundary: (i) reversibility — can this action be undone in \(30\) seconds by closing a tab, or does it persist (email sent, file deleted, record written to an EHR)?; and (ii) human-in-the-loop — did a human read the agent’s reasoning before the action happened?. A mode is “safe by default” if it is either reversible or human-in-the-loop; it is “dangerous by default” if it is neither (i.e. do stuff on an irreversible target without a confirm step).
Place the trust boundary in a small clinical-research workflow: given a multi-step task (e.g. “find the latest guidelines, summarise them, draft a one-page protocol, email it to the PI”), decide for each step whether the agent may act autonomously, must ask, must share, or must hand back — and justify the boundary using the reversibility criterion (“I let the agent search, summarise, and draft autonomously because all three are reversible; I require an ask-step before sending the email because email is irreversible”).



10 · Best practices for ML projects · 15 min
By the end of this chapter, students can:

Plan a first iteration of an ML project as the simplest model on the smallest sensible feature set, and write an explicit stop-criterion before adding complexity. Concretely, given a problem and a dataset, state (a) the baseline model (e.g. logistic regression on \(5\)–\(10\) features), (b) the baseline metric and the target value that would make the simple model “good enough”, and (c) the single failure mode that would justify increasing model complexity — and not before. State the rationale in one sentence: more parameters and richer features are paid for in robustness, interpretability, and risk of overfitting — so each added unit of complexity must be earned by a failure of the simpler model.
Choose metrics for the problem you actually have, not for the problem accuracy assumes you have. Apply two rules: (R1) on an imbalanced problem with positive-class prevalence \(p\) (e.g. \(p = 1\%\), a rare event), reporting accuracy is misleading because the always-predict-majority classifier reaches accuracy \(= 1 - p = 99\%\) while being clinically useless — use precision, recall, F1, or AUPRC instead, and pick the threshold deliberately based on the clinical cost of false positives vs false negatives. (R2) the data-leakage rule: any decision (model choice, hyperparameter, feature set, threshold) that is taken after having seen a performance number on a dataset converts that dataset into a training set — even if the file is labelled “test”. A faithful test set is one that has been looked at exactly once, at the end, and never again.
Match the interpretability technique to the model family, and weigh the interpretability/performance tradeoff in a healthcare deployment context. The mapping: linear / logistic regression → read off the coefficients (each one is the log-odds change per unit of feature, with sign and magnitude); decision tree → read off the decision path (a sequence of human-readable if-then rules); random forest / gradient boosting → use variable importance (which features the ensemble relies on most); neural network / deep model → use SHAP (per-sample additive attribution) or surrogate models. State the operational rule for healthcare: if the deployment requires clinical defensibility (e.g. a clinician must justify a single recommendation to a patient), prefer a model whose interpretability is built-in (linear or single tree) — unless the performance gap to the opaque model is large enough that the patient is better off with the box-with-SHAP than with a simpler model that misclassifies more often. The tradeoff is a clinical decision, not a technical one.

Total contact time: 225 min.

text: Module 2 · Practice — Basic (≈4h)

title: Schedule & Planning
text:
Steps

Step 00 — Setup · 25 min
Initialise a reproducible RStudio project from scratch with renv and here.


Step 01 — Import & wrangle · 35 min
Import the heart-failure data and wrangle it tidily, dropping the leaky follow-up column.


Step 02 — Clinical EDA · 30 min
Explore the cohort with clinically meaningful summaries (gtsummary).


Step 03 — Logistic spine · 45 min
Fit a logistic-regression spine and score it on two metrics — AUC-ROC and AUC-PR.


Step 04 — The zoo, tuned · 70 min
Tune and compare a small model zoo with a workflow_set, then validate the winner with last_fit.


Step 05 — Reproducible report · 35 min
Wrap the whole analysis in a reproducible Quarto report.
Total contact time: 240 min.
